item.title: Fitch on UK Budget: Policy continuity leaves a tough delivery challenge
item.description:
Fitch’s assessment of the UK Budget points to a familiar problem: setting out a path to stronger public finances is one thing. Delivering it is another.

The ratings agency sees broad continuity in government policy, but warns that the plans still leave a sizeable delivery challenge. It continues to anticipate significant slippage against spending plans and says fiscal consolidation becomes much more challenging to deliver from 2027.

That puts the emphasis on execution. The key barometer will be whether actual spending and borrowing follow the government’s projected path.

Spending discipline remains the central concern

Fitch’s warning about spending slippage suggests it expects the government to struggle to keep expenditure within its planned limits.

If spending exceeds those assumptions, the government would need to offset the difference through higher revenues, savings elsewhere or additional borrowing. Each carries consequences for the economic outlook and the credibility of the fiscal plan.

For investors, the question is whether the projected improvement in public finances can survive the pressures that emerge along the way.

Election politics add another layer of risk

Fitch also sees moderately greater policy risk closer to the next general election.

The implication is that the political willingness to deliver difficult fiscal measures could weaken as an election approaches. Pressure to support households, protect public services or offer new commitments could complicate the planned adjustment.

That matters because Fitch already sees the consolidation becoming harder from 2027. The economic and political challenges could increasingly overlap.

Investment measures do not materially change the picture

Fitch notes that support through the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank will increase. However, it does not see the Burnham government as meaningfully lifting its infrastructure spending plans.

It also expects measures allowing mayors to spend a portion of income tax revenues from 2028 to be broadly fiscally neutral initially.

Those initiatives therefore do little to change Fitch’s central concern: the difficulty of delivering the overall fiscal path.

The market takeaway

My reading is that this is a warning about delivery and credibility. Broad policy continuity provides a framework, but the spending numbers still have to hold.

For gilt and sterling traders, these headlines identify a risk to monitor rather than establish a market direction on their own. If confidence in the fiscal path deteriorates, upward pressure on borrowing costs could become a concern. Sterling’s response would depend on whether higher yields reflect stronger economic expectations or greater fiscal risk.

The budget sets the targets. The spending and borrowing data will show whether the government can deliver.

As a review, the UK Budget was delivered on Wednesday, October 28. Its main aim was to provide targeted cost-of-living relief while preserving plans to reduce borrowing, with difficult spending decisions still ahead.

  • Household support: A £100 energy payment for eligible households in England’s council tax bands A–D, with funding for comparable support elsewhere in the UK. The electricity VAT cut and temporary 5p fuel-duty reduction are extended until July 2027.
  • Targeted tax increases: The bank corporation tax surcharge rises temporarily from 3% to 6%. From April 2027, tax rates on savings and property income will be 24%, 44% and 49%.
  • Wages and businesses: The National Living Wage rises 3.9% to £13.21 an hour in April 2027. Retail, hospitality and leisure businesses receive expanded business-rate relief.
  • Housing: An additional £1.5 billion supports social and affordable housing, alongside a new equity-loan scheme for first-time buyers and a First Time Buyer ISA from April 2029.
  • Weaker growth, higher inflation: The OBR cut its 2027 growth forecast to 1.0% from 1.6%, while raising its inflation forecast to 3.4% from 2.0%. It judged that the budget measures make little difference to those forecasts.
  • Limited fiscal room: The government meets its fiscal rules on the forecasts, but the buffer against its day-to-day budget target is only £15 billion in 2029/30. Borrowing is projected to average approximately £13 billion a year more than previously forecast over 2026/27–2030/31.

THE GBPUSD has moved higher this week after bottoming on Wednesday

Technically, the GBPUSD bottomed on Wednesday near the swing level at 1.32729, giving buyers a technical floor to lean against. The subsequent recovery initially attracted sellers near the falling 100-hour moving average, but buyers broke through that resistance during yesterday’s trade and extended above the 200-hour moving average.

Those breaks shifted the near-term bias toward the buyers. The 100-hour moving average at 1.3338 and the 200-hour moving average at 1.33585 became support levels to watch on a correction.

Buyers reach the 200-day moving average

The rally gathered momentum today, with the price breaking above two additional hurdles:

  • 100-day moving average: 1.33857

  • 50% midpoint of the decline from the August high: 1.34056

Those breaks opened the door for a test of the 200-day moving average at 1.34277. The session high reached 1.3433, taking the price modestly above that longer-term barometer.

However, buyers could not sustain the break. Sellers leaned against the area, and the price rotated lower during the North American session.

That makes the 200-day moving average an important ceiling. Buyers reached a major target, but they still need to establish acceptance above it to strengthen the bullish case.

The pullback puts buyers to the test

The rotation lower has taken the price back below the 50% midpoint at 1.34056 and the 100-day moving average at 1.33857. Giving back those breaks takes some of the momentum out of the rally and gives sellers an opportunity to regain control.

The 1.33857 level becomes the immediate barometer. Staying below it would keep sellers in play and leave the 200-hour moving average at 1.33585 as the next downside target. Below that, the 100-hour moving average at 1.3338 would come into focus.

Conversely, a move back above 1.33857, followed by 1.34056, would help buyers steady the technical picture and put the 1.34277–1.3433 resistance area back in their sights.

The recovery from Wednesday’s low has cleared several important hurdles. The question now is how much of that technical progress buyers can defend.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold tumbles despite lower yields. Technicals show the way.
item.description:
Lower yields fail to provide support

Gold is moving sharply lower despite a decline in US Treasury yields. The 10-year yield is down 5 basis points to 4.939%, a move that would normally provide some support for the precious metal. Instead, gold is trading near $3900, down roughly $120, or 3%, after reaching a session low near $3891.

That divergence is telling. Buyers have a potentially supportive move in the bond market, but they are struggling to turn it into buying momentum. When the price cannot rally on a favorable development, traders need to respect what the price action is saying.

Connecting the dots from a fundamental or interest-rate perspective may be difficult. The technicals, however, are providing a clearer roadmap.

Moving averages put sellers in control

On the hourly chart, gold moved back below its 100- and 200-hour moving averages on October 19. The downside did not accelerate immediately, but those moving averages helped form a ceiling, keeping the bearish bias intact. By October 22, downside momentum began to build.

The subsequent decline took the price to $3959.37 before buyers managed a recovery. However, that rebound stalled on Wednesday near $4080, against the 200-hour moving average.

That failed recovery was an important clue. Buyers had an opportunity to challenge the bearish bias, but they could not push through a key technical barometer. Sellers could lean against the moving average with defined risk—and the subsequent rotation lower rewarded that decision.

A broken floor accelerates the decline

The next leg lower has continued into today with little sustained upside correction. Once the price broke below the $3942.71–$3959.37 swing area, selling accelerated, taking gold toward $3891.

That break matters because an established support area gives traders a reference point. Above it, buyers have a floor to lean against. Below it, those buyers face pressure to exit, while sellers gain another level against which to define risk.

The former floor now becomes a ceiling to watch on a recovery.

Channel support gives buyers a foothold

Today’s low stalled near a lower channel trendline on the hourly chart. Buyers have leaned against that support, producing a modest bounce, with the price now trading above and below $3900.

Holding the trendline gives buyers an opportunity to slow the decline and attempt a corrective recovery. It also provides a close risk level: if support breaks, the reason for buying against it weakens.

A bounce alone, however, does not change the broader bearish picture. Buyers need to reclaim resistance to demonstrate that they can take back some control.

What next? Watch support below and the broken swing area above

If buyers can keep the price above the lower channel trendline, the next upside target is the $3942.71–$3959.37 swing area. Expect that zone to act as a test of the recovery. Sellers may lean against it, while a move back above would strengthen the buyers’ case and take some pressure off the downside.

Conversely, a break below the trendline and today’s low near $3891 would open the door to another extension lower.

Sellers retain control. Buyers have support to lean against, but they still have something to prove. The trendline defines the immediate downside risk, while the broken swing area defines the next upside hurdle.

In the video above, I walk through those levels and explain how they help define the bias, risk, and targets for gold’s next move.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nasdaq leads stocks lower as investors question the cost of AI growth
item.description:
US stocks are trading lower, with the Nasdaq indices taking the biggest hit as investors reassess the earnings outlook—and the cost of delivering on the AI growth story.

  • Dow: Down 176.04 points, or 0.34%, at 52,172.21.

  • S&P 500: Down 88.50 points, or 1.15%, at 7,631.89.

  • Nasdaq Composite: Down 569.26 points, or 2.17%, at 25,615.47.

  • Russell 2000: Down 18.92 points, or 0.66%, at 2,840.30.

  • Nasdaq 100: Down 752.25 points, or 2.56%, at 28,650.25.

The selling highlights a shift in what investors are willing to reward. Strong AI growth remains important, but the market is becoming more demanding about what that growth costs, when the investment will generate returns, and how much cash is left along the way.

Amazon and Intel both reported after yesterday’s close, and both disappointed investors. The concerns differ, but the reports leave buyers facing the same question: Does the outlook justify the stock price?

Amazon: Strong growth comes with a heavy spending bill

For Amazon, the concern centers on spending and cash flow. AWS continues to grow strongly, but building the infrastructure to support that demand requires enormous capital investment. That spending absorbs cash generated by the business, while a softer holiday sales outlook adds uncertainty about the consumer.

Investors want a clearer path from AI demand to sustainable cash flow. Growth matters, but so does the cost of delivering it.

Technically, sellers have taken the price below two important reference points: the 200-day moving average at $243.38 and the 50% midpoint of the rally from the February low at $241.60. The stock is currently trading near $233.22.

Those breaks weaken the technical picture and turn the $241.60–$243.38 area into overhead resistance. Buyers need to reclaim that area to begin repairing the damage. Until then, a bounce would leave the price below those key technical levels, with sellers maintaining the advantage.

Intel: An earnings beat fails to offset concerns about the recovery

For Intel, the concern is the durability of its recovery. The company beat earnings expectations, but disappointing forward guidance shifted attention toward the challenges ahead. Weak PC demand, manufacturing constraints and continued heavy investment create hurdles for the coming quarters.

An earnings beat can attract attention. The outlook helps determine whether buyers stick around.

Intel shares are getting hammered, falling approximately 28.6% to $66, their lowest level since April. Despite that decline, the stock remains well above its year-end level near $37.50. However, it has surrendered a substantial portion of a rally that took the price as high as $142.35 this year.

That is a sharp reminder of how quickly an elevated share price can become vulnerable when expectations for future growth are marked down.

The AI trade faces a tougher test

Together, the reports challenge an important assumption behind the technology rally: that strong AI demand will be enough to support higher stock prices.

Demand can remain strong while the spending needed to meet it weighs on cash flow and profitability. When expectations are already elevated, investors have less patience for uncertainty about the timing and size of future returns.

The fundamental concerns are also being reinforced by technical breaks. Both the Nasdaq Composite and Nasdaq 100 fell below their 100-day moving averages yesterday. Today’s gaps lower have broken additional support, giving sellers more control and leaving buyers with work to do.

Nasdaq Composite: Another support break opens the door lower

The Nasdaq Composite broke below its 100-day moving average near 26,252 yesterday, closing at 26,184.72.

Today, the index has gapped below its next key technical level at 25,831.74. At the opening snapshot above, it was trading at 25,615.47, down 2.17%.

With that support broken, the next major downside focus shifts toward the 25,035 area, where the rising 200-day moving average and the 38.2% retracement are clustered. The combination makes that area an important barometer if the selling continues. Buyers may look to lean against it, with risk defined by whether the support holds or breaks.

What would improve the picture before then?

The first step would be to get back above—and stay above—25,831.74. That would begin to question today’s break lower. Beyond that, buyers would need to reclaim the 100-day moving average near 26,252 to take back more control.

Until those levels are recovered, sellers retain the technical advantage.

Nasdaq 100: The old floor becomes a key resistance area

The Nasdaq 100 also broke below its 100-day moving average near 29,559.71 yesterday, falling 1.38% to close at 29,402.51.

Today’s gap lower has taken the index below a key swing area between 28,822 and 28,953. At the opening snapshot above, the index was trading at 28,650.25, down 2.56%.

The break matters because an area that previously attracted buyers now becomes a test for any recovery. If the price rallies toward that old floor and sellers lean against it, the bearish bias would remain intact.

On the downside, the next major target is the 38.2% retracement of the rally from the April low at 28,108, followed by the rising 200-day moving average at 27,894.40.

For buyers, the first task is to reclaim the 28,822–28,953 swing area and establish support above it. That would help stabilize the near-term picture. A recovery above the 100-day moving average near 29,559.71 would be needed to make a stronger case that buyers are regaining control.

For now, the earnings concerns have given investors a reason to sell, and the technical breaks have given sellers added confidence. Buyers need to reclaim the broken levels to challenge that control.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed's Barkin: Direction of travel is straightforward for the Fed
item.description:
Comments from the Fed’s Barkin cross the wires:

  • Direction of travel is “straightforward” for the Fed, the question is pace.
  • A gradual approach is a good way to go right now.
  • A lot of cost pressures are hitting American businesses.
  • In the context of years of elevated inflation it is easier for businesses to argue they need to raise prices.
  • Resilience of consumer spending has been a surprise given relatively flat incomes.
  • The AI investment surge has pressured supply chains, and that is inflationary.
  • AI investment is leading to demand side inflation, which is the kind of thing the Fed can lean against.
  • Businesses are saying that there cost pressures are broad-based.
  • Businesses are laying plans to pass those costs on to their customers.
  • Demand remains a solid with only weakness in nonprofits and in the housing sector

Analysis: Barkin’s comments carry a hawkish bias, but with a preference for moving gradually. The key distinction is his view that AI investment is generating demand that the Fed can lean against. Strong investment spending and pressure on supply chains could keep inflation elevated, even as relatively flat incomes would normally be expected to restrain consumers.

For policy expectations, the question is how quickly the Fed needs to respond. Barkin favors a measured approach, but resilient spending and businesses finding it easier to pass along higher costs suggest continued concern about inflation persistence. His remarks do not specify the size or timing of the next move.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bitcoin sellers jump on the risk-off bandwagon
item.description:
With US and European stocks moving lower, bitcoin is following the risk-off sentiment. However, the move also has a technical catalyst: a break below the consolidation range that had contained the price since October 22.

That range extended from $79,146 on the downside to $81,930 on the topside. Over the last 24 hours, sellers pushed through the floor, triggering downside momentum that carried the price to $76,320.

The break gave sellers more control. The question now is whether they can extend that advantage through the next key support area.

Buyers find a reason to lean against support

The low stalled about $174 above the rising 100-day moving average at $76,146. Just below that moving average sits the 38.2% retracement of the advance from the late-June low at $76,052.

Together, those levels create a support zone between $76,052 and $76,146.

When two technical measures converge, they give traders a more clearly defined area to assess the next move. Dip buyers can lean against that support with limited risk, provided they are prepared to exit if the price breaks below and stays below it.

That does not guarantee a lasting bottom. It gives buyers a location where the potential reward can be weighed against a defined risk.

The initial rebound carried bitcoin to $78,559, but buyers could not sustain the recovery. The price has since rotated back toward $77,208, keeping the support zone in focus.

The old floor becomes the upside barometer

For buyers, holding support is only the first step. They also need to reclaim broken resistance.

The key level is $79,146, the former floor of the consolidation range. A break below support often turns that same level into resistance as sellers lean against it and trapped buyers use a rebound to exit.

As long as bitcoin stays below $79,146, sellers retain the advantage from the breakdown. A recovery above that level—and an ability to stay above it—would raise the possibility of a failed break lower.

That would start to worry sellers looking for further downside and put the upper boundary of the old range at $81,930 back on the radar.

Before then, the rebound high at $78,559 provides an interim upside hurdle.

Sellers need to break the support confluence

For sellers, the next task is clear: push below the 100-day moving average at $76,146 and the 38.2% retracement at $76,052, then keep the price below that area.

The 38.2% retracement is an important barometer when assessing a correction within a broader advance. Holding above it keeps the pullback relatively contained. Breaking below it would strengthen the case that a deeper correction is developing.

A brief move below support followed by a quick recovery would be less convincing. Sellers need sustained trading below the zone to confirm that the next downside break has traction.

Let the levels define the risk

War uncertainty, inflation concerns, worries about slower growth, and falling stock markets make the bearish case easy to understand. The break away from the 100- and 200-hour moving averages, followed by the move below consolidation support, adds technical weight to that story.

Nevertheless, a bearish narrative still needs a risk level.

For sellers, $79,146 is the key upside barometer. A sustained recovery above it would weaken the breakdown.

For dip buyers, $76,052–$76,146 is the key support zone. A sustained break below it would undermine the argument for buying against that confluence.

The battle lines are drawn. Sellers control the price below the old floor, while buyers have a defined support area where they can attempt to slow—or reverse—the decline.

In the video above, I walk through the breakdown, the support confluence, and what buyers and sellers need to see next to strengthen their respective cases.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Crude oil extends gains as traders hedge into weekend amid risks of US strikes on Iran
item.description:
Crude oil extended the gains into new highs yesterday after the Houthis targeted the Aramco oil company in widespread wave of missile attacks.

The bullish momentum then accelerated after the Wall Street Journal reported that in a rare in-person visit to the White House, the top US commander in the Middle East briefed Trump on military options for Iran as the US weighed resuming major combat operations.

This is the last weekend before the US midterm elections, so there’s some concern of a US attack over the weekend. We might see some hedging going into the weekend that could push oil prices even higher.

The market remains supported amid the Saudi-Houthi conflict and the possibility of renewed US strikes. We would need a de-escalation in the Saudi-Houthi conflict or a surprising breakthrough in US-Iran negotiations to get a significant correction in oil prices.

Keep also in mind that the market could take another US attack as an exit strategy, so after the initial spike we could see traders unwinding bullish bets. But that will depend on what Trump says after the potential attack and how strong Iran’s retaliation is going to be.

If we don’t see any attack this weekend, oil prices could open lower on Monday and what happens next, will depend on further Middle East developments.

 

CRUDE OIL TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

On the daily chart, we can see that crude oil(CFD contract) extended the gains into new highs as fears of an imminent US strikes on Iran grew. Technically, there’s not much we can glean from this timeframe as the most important levels remain the lower bound of the channel and the resistance around the 110.00 level, so we need to zoom in to see some more details.

CRUDE OIL TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 4 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 4 hour chart, we have the upward trendline defining the bullish momentum. The buyers continue to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk below it, to keep pushing into new highs. The sellers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking lower to pile in for a correction into the lower bound of the channel.

CRUDE OIL TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 1 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 1 hour chart, there’s not much we can add here as the buyers will continue to have a better risk to reward setup around the trendline, while the sellers will need a break below it to open the door for new lows. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

item.title: US employment cost index for Q3 +0.8% vs +0.8% expected
item.description:
• Prior quarter was +0.9%
  • Employment benefits +0.9% vs +1.0% prior quarter
  • Employment wages +0.7% vs +0.9% prior quarter

The US Employment Cost Index (ECI) increased by 0.8% q/q in the third quarter, with both wages and salaries and benefit costs contributing to the increase. Wages and salaries rose 0.7%, while benefit costs increased 0.9% compared with the previous quarter.

On an annual basis, total compensation costs for civilian workers increased by 3.4%, with wages and salaries rising 3.1% and benefit costs accelerating by 3.9%. The figures show that labour cost pressures remain relatively contained, although benefits continue to increase faster than wages.

Looking at private industry, compensation costs also increased by 0.8% q/q and 3.4% y/y. However, inflation-adjusted wages and salaries declined by 0.6% over the year, as nominal wage growth is still failing to keep pace with consumer price increases. The continued gap between nominal and inflation-adjusted wage growth also highlights the pressure households are facing from higher living costs.

For background, the Employment Cost Index (ECI) is a quarterly report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) that measures the change in the total cost of labor for businesses. The Fed considers the ECI the "gold standard" for measuring wage inflation because it is more precise and comprehensive, the only drawback is that it's not as timely as the Average Hourly Earnings data.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Canada GDP for August 0.0% vs 0.2% estimate
item.description:
• Prior Month 0.0%

Details of the Canada GDP for the month of August:

  • August real GDP: 0.0% MoM. Prior 0.0%.

  • September advance estimate: -0.1% MoM.

  • Q3 preliminary growth indication: +0.3% QoQ, not annualized.

  • Breadth: 9 of 20 industrial sectors expanded in August.

  • Services-producing industries: -0.1%.

  • Goods-producing industries: +0.1%.

Key August sector details:

  • Retail trade: +1.2%, led by motor vehicle and parts dealers.

  • Manufacturing: +0.3%, supported by machinery and petroleum refining.

  • Wholesale trade: -1.4%, the largest drag on growth.

  • Public sector: -0.2%, partly reflecting the winding down of Census work.

  • Oil and gas extraction: -1.2%, its third consecutive monthly decline.

  • Utilities: -0.4%, weighed down by nuclear maintenance outages.

Canada’s economy stalled for a second consecutive month in August, according to Statistics Canada’s gross domestic product (GDP) by industry report. The softer detail came in the forward estimate: output is projected to have declined 0.1% in September, suggesting the economy lost momentum heading into the end of the third quarter. The industry-based figures point to 0.3% quarterly growth in Q3, subject to confirmation in the official quarterly release.

August’s flat headline masked considerable movement underneath. Retail trade rebounded 1.2%, more than reversing July’s contraction, while machinery production and a recovery in petroleum refining supported manufacturing. Those gains were offset by weaker wholesale trade, lower public-sector activity and another decline in oil and gas extraction. Auto production was particularly weak, with motor vehicles and parts manufacturing down 5.8% amid a prolonged summer plant shutdown.

Quick analysis: Two flat months followed by a projected decline suggest an economy struggling to build momentum. The retail rebound is encouraging, but growth was narrow, with fewer than half of industrial sectors expanding. Some weakness reflects maintenance outages, auto shutdowns and the winding down of Census activity, which limits how much can be attributed to softer underlying demand.

For the Bank of Canada, the growth figures could strengthen the case for easier policy if inflation allows. In isolation, weaker growth would normally weigh on Canadian yields and the Canadian dollar, creating an upward bias for USDCAD. The next checkpoint is November 30, when September GDP and the official Q3 income-and-expenditure estimates are released.

What this report measures: GDP by industry tracks inflation-adjusted production across Canada’s economy. Monthly changes show whether activity is expanding or contracting and which industries are driving it. The advance estimate is preliminary and subject to revision; the official quarterly income-and-expenditure report provides a separate measure of overall growth.

Looking at the USDCAD chart below, the price of the USDCAD moved lower with the USD, but after testing the 61.8% of the move up  from the August low, is boucing modestly.   That level comes in at 1.39497.  The price, however, needs to get and stay above the high of the swing area at 1.3963 to give the dip buyers at the 61.8% some hope.  

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Morning Kickstart: Tech hammered as Amazon and Intel tumble; oil rises despite peace talk
item.description:
Technology stocks are taking another hit heading into Friday’s North American session. Disappointing earnings from Amazon and a sharp negative reaction to Intel’s results are adding to concerns about the spending, profitability and expectations surrounding the AI trade.

The weakness is concentrated in technology, with Nasdaq futures down 785 points and S&P futures down 84 points, while Dow futures are holding a modest 15-point gain. That divergence matters. Technology is leading the pressure, while the Dow is showing greater resilience.

Elsewhere, the U.S. dollar is mostly lower and Treasury yields are falling across the curve. Crude oil, however, is moving higher despite President Trump’s optimistic comments about an end to the Iran war. The combination leaves traders balancing weaker technology sentiment against an energy market that continues to signal concern.

Amazon and Intel deepen the technology selloff

Amazon missed expectations for both earnings and revenue. Intel beat adjusted EPS estimates but missed revenue expectations, and its shares are suffering a much larger decline.

The broader question for investors remains: Are the earnings and future cash flows strong enough to justify the spending and valuations associated with AI?

An earnings beat alone does not guarantee a positive stock reaction. Investors also assess guidance, margins, capital spending and how much good news was already reflected in the share price. Sandisk’s decline despite beating both supplied estimates illustrates that distinction.

The earnings comparisons and early share reactions are currently showing:

  • Intel: Adjusted EPS $0.52 vs $0.41 (BEAT); revenue $16.50 billion vs $16.60 billion (MISS). Shares down 25.70%.

  • Amazon: EPS $1.89 vs $1.97 (MISS); revenue $201.90 billion vs $202.20 billion (MISS). Shares down 6.68%.

  • Gilead Sciences: Adjusted EPS $2.55 vs $2.19 (BEAT); revenue $8.30 billion vs $7.80 billion (BEAT). Shares up 4.41%.

  • Sandisk: Adjusted EPS $49.51 vs $46.20 (BEAT); revenue $11.031 billion vs $10.639 billion (BEAT). Shares down 8.20%.

  • Starbucks: Adjusted EPS $0.80 vs $0.72 (BEAT); revenue $9.10 billion vs $9.22 billion (MISS). Shares up 0.30%.

  • Pinterest: Revenue $1.17 billion vs $1.21 billion (MISS). Shares down 8.18%.

U.S. stock-index futures:

  • Dow industrial average futures: Up 15 points.

  • S&P 500 futures: Down 84 points.

  • Nasdaq 100 futures: Down 785 points.

ECB officials: Yesterday’s hold leaves further hikes in play

The morning after the ECB left rates unchanged, officials are reinforcing the message that the inflation battle is unfinished. The common thread is a willingness to tighten further, with differences over how quickly action may be needed and how much tightening financial markets are already delivering.

Martin Kocher — a conditional warning about further tightening

Kocher said inflation risks have clearly increased and that a monetary policy response will be necessary if conditions do not improve soon. His comments suggest limited patience with persistent inflation pressure, while acknowledging the risks of acting prematurely.

The message for traders: yesterday’s unchanged decision should not be interpreted as confidence that inflation is under control.

Fabio Panetta — further hikes may be needed, but bond yields matter

Panetta said more rate increases may be necessary and warned that the increase in core inflation could become more pronounced early next year. However, he also stressed that the ECB must consider the recent rise in longer-term bond yields when calibrating policy.

Higher market borrowing costs can restrain demand without an additional ECB hike. Panetta also left room to adjust policy promptly if international conditions improve or financial tensions slow inflation.

His message is conditional: further tightening remains possible, but the ECB must assess how much restraint is already working through the economy.

Joachim Nagel — ready to act, with limited second-round effects so far

Nagel said policymakers would act decisively if needed, while noting that significant second-round effects have not appeared thus far.

That distinction matters. An energy-price shock can lift headline inflation directly. The greater concern is whether businesses and workers respond in ways that embed higher inflation in broader prices and wages.

The overall ECB message: The hold preserves flexibility, but further hikes remain an option. Persistent core inflation would strengthen the case for action, while higher bond yields and an improvement in the energy outlook could reduce the need for additional tightening.

Trump talks up an end to the Iran war, but oil moves higher (and the stocks are tumbling ahead of the election next week)

President Trump said in an interview this morning that the Iran war would end very soon, “one way or another,” and that gasoline prices would decline.

Separately, in a Truth Social post, he asserted that inflation is way down under his administration and that incomes for people and companies are higher. Those are the president’s claims; traders will continue to judge the inflation outlook through incoming data and energy prices.

The attached Al Arabiya report, citing sources, says the U.S. has informed mediators that Iran abandoning its nuclear programme is the basis for negotiations. Mediators are reportedly discussing access for inspectors to Iran’s nuclear sites in exchange for the release of some frozen funds.

That points to diplomatic discussions, but it does not establish an agreement. The gap between discussing terms and securing an enforceable settlement remains important for markets.

For now, crude is moving in the opposite direction to the president’s anticipated price relief. WTI is at $104.13, up $2.13 or 2.09%. The price action suggests traders still require evidence of an improvement in the supply and security outlook.

U.S. dollar lower against most major currencies

The dollar is lower against six of the seven major currencies in the snapshot, with the Australian dollar unchanged.

The Swiss franc is the strongest against the dollar, followed by the Japanese yen and British pound. The Australian dollar is the weakest performer within this group, holding flat.

The hack raised concerns about exchange security and potential contagion across the crypto ecosystem. Although Binance pledged to cover customer losses, uncertainty surrounding the stolen assets and potential liquidations weighed on sentiment.

Around $1.53 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated over 24 hours. While the Binance hack triggered the initial shock, leveraged positioning and cascading liquidations magnified the losses.

Historically, cryptocurrency selloffs triggered by exchange hacks have often been followed by a recovery, but the economic context decided how quickly. The initial reaction tends to be driven by panic, uncertainty and forced liquidations rather than a deterioration in the fundamentals of cryptocurrencies.

The macro picture is still largely bearish given inflation risks, growth concerns, risk-off sentiment, upcoming rate hikes and geopolitical tensions. item.title: Italy October preliminary CPI +5.4% vs +4.6% y/y expected
item.description:
• Prior +4.2%
  • HICP +5.6% vs +4.6% y/y expected
  • Prior +4.2%

Inflation accelerated sharply in October 2026, but the increase was primarily driven by energy prices, with both regulated and non-regulated energy products recording significant increases. Regulated energy inflation surged from 25.8% to 59.5% y/y, while non-regulated energy prices accelerated from 22.5% to 29.4%. Higher energy costs remain the dominant driver of the inflationary shock.

However, price pressures were not limited to energy. Unprocessed food inflation accelerated from 5.5% to 7.5%, while processed food prices also returned to positive annual growth. Services inflation picked up more modestly, rising to 2.9% from 2.6%, with transport-related services accelerating to 3.1%.

The goods component was particularly notable, with annual inflation jumping to 7.5% from 5.4%, while services inflation remained considerably more contained. This suggests that the latest acceleration is still heavily concentrated in goods and energy-related costs rather than reflecting an equally broad-based increase across the services sector.

Overall, the data points to significant inflationary shock in Italy, largely driven by surging energy costs but increasingly spilling over into food and transportation prices.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Eurozone Q3 GDP beats expectations but the growth surprise comes with a catch
item.description:
• Eurozone Q3 preliminary GDP +0.4% vs +0.2% q/q expected
  • Prior +0.6%
  • Eurozone Q3 preliminary GDP +1.3% vs +1.1% y/y expected
  • Prior +1.2%

Well, well, well. Would you look at that. The euro area economy has managed to pull a rabbit out of the hat, delivering a better-than-expected Q3 GDP reading at first glance. But before we start popping the champagne, there's a catch or two worth considering when you look at the details.

To start, quarterly growth did still slow down to 0.4% in the third quarter - down from 0.6% in the second quarter. So while the headline surprise is encouraging, the underlying momentum isn't quite as impressive as it might seem.

And when you drill deeper into the details, that is when things start to get a bit more interesting.

Of note, Ireland leads the pack with a whopping 5.5% quarterly expansion in Q3. Having said that, Ireland has a knack for notoriously volatile GDP figures in the past year and that always warrants some caution. The expansion here was primarily driven by strong activity in multinational-dominated industries, specifically information and communication and manufacturing.

For some context, Ireland's headline growth figure is often a distorted gauge of domestic economic health. That is because it is heavily influenced by contract manufacturing and global profits of multinational corporations that largely flow back to foreign shareholders rather than translating directly into local living standards.

Besides that, Spain continues to punch above its weight with 0.6% growth while the Netherlands also posted a respectable 0.6% increase.

Elsewhere though? The picture isn't so pretty.

Germany managed just 0.2% growth, Italy stagnated at 0.0%, and France even contracted by 0.1%. Now, that's hardly an endorsement of economic resilience across the biggest economies in the region.

So, what does this mean for the ECB?

We've seen inflation pressures heating up in France and Spain today even as the growth picture remains rather uneven. Meanwhile, German state inflation readings offered some relief but the broader concern remains that higher energy costs would eventually feed through to prices while weighing on economic activity.

And that is precisely the kind of stagflationary squeeze policymakers would want to avoid at this juncture.

So the real question now is whether the euro area can maintain its growth momentum as higher prices are going to squeeze households and businesses more and more in the months ahead. The latest report today might suggest that growth conditions are holding up a little bit better than feared, but whether that remains the case heading into Q4 will be a different story altogether.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold gets hit again by forced liquidations as equity losses mount; fundamental outlook increasingly positive
item.description:
Gold came under renewed pressure yesterday as another selloff in equities weighed on precious metals. Gold has been tightly correlated with the stock market recently, with the latest losses seemingly driven by investors liquidating positions to cover losses elsewhere in their portfolios.

Chart: You can see the correlation between the Nasdaq (blue line) and gold (candlesticks)

To understand the mechanics, imagine that an investment fund holds stocks, gold and government bonds. Some stocks suddenly crash, and the fund suffers losses on leveraged positions. The fund may need to raise cash to meet margin calls, reduce leverage or satisfy investor redemptions. Rather than selling only the assets that caused the losses, it may sell whatever it can liquidate quickly. Gold is particularly useful in this situation because it is highly liquid and can be sold quickly.

The main drivers like real yields have been actually pointing to higher gold prices. In fact, real yields fell significantly as inflation expectations remain roughly unchanged given the increase in oil prices, while nominal Treasury yields fell as the losses in the stock market triggered a flight to safety.

We can also see the unusual divergence between spot gold and the ETFs holdings in the chart below. Generally speaking, spot prices lead ETFs inflows and outflows, but in this case, I think it’s technical factors capping the upside in gold, not fundamental ones.

Once the artificial selling stops weighing on gold, we could see a strong and quick rebound. We are also approaching a generally favourable seasonal period between December and January. The hard part is timing. Traders could lean on key technical levels or wait for a fundamental catalyst. item.title: German state inflation cools in October, but will that ease the ECB's headache?
item.description:
The state readings released around the same time:

  • Bavaria September CPI +2.8% vs +3.2% y/y prior
  • Saxony September CPI +2.9% vs +3.3% y/y prior
  • North Rhine Westphalia September CPI +2.7% vs +3.3% y/y prior
  • Baden Wuerttemberg September CPI +2.6% vs +2.9% y/y prior

After the acceleration in September, headline inflation is seen cooling back a little in German states. While base effects are part of the reason, the re-implementation of specific energy tax reductions and fuel discounts enacted at the start of the month are arguably also playing a part here.

So, that is leading to cooler price pressures overall but still relatively elevated when compared to the months before this.

Putting the estimates together, it offers an indication that German inflation is set to decline at the national level as well. Headline annual inflation is expected to drop to 3.0% in October from 3.3% last month, with the state readings above pointing to a modest likelihood that we might even see a reading below the 3% mark.

In any case, just keep in mind though that the state readings aren't a perfect proxy for the national figure. There can still be some deviation when the preliminary numbers are released later. However, they have historically been a useful gauge and today's readings arguably point to some downside risk to the 3.0% consensus, with a national CPI reading around 2.9% now looking quite plausible.

For the ECB, the readings here will just complicate things further as the economic backdrop is reflecting flagging growth conditions amid the risk of price pressures accelerating further. While German inflation may not have jumped in October, there are signs elsewhere that inflation is starting to spread more broadly as seen with France and Spain earlier.

So, that will just keep the pressure on policymakers to act again in December while having to consider if doing too much could risk sending the euro area economy over the edge.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Italy Q3 preliminary GDP +0.0% vs +0.1% q/q expected
item.description:
• Prior +0.2%
  • GDP Y/Y +0.8% vs +0.9% y/y expected
  • Prior +1.0%

Italy's economy unexpectedly stalled in the third quarter of 2026, with GDP remaining unchanged q/q, following 0.2% growth in the previous quarter. On an annual basis, GDP increased by 0.8%, pointing to a relatively modest pace of economic expansion.

On the supply side, services and agriculture provided positive contributions to growth, while industrial activity declined. The weakness in industry remains a concern, particularly given the sector's importance to Italy's export-oriented economy.

On the demand side, domestic demand, including changes in inventories, supported economic activity, while net foreign demand acted as a drag. This suggests that domestic spending continues to provide some resilience, but external demand and trade flows remain a source of weakness.

The carry-over growth rate for 2026 stands at 0.8% on a calendar-adjusted basis. This means that even if GDP remains unchanged in the fourth quarter, annual growth would still be around 0.8%, although the final annual figure may differ due to the three additional working days in 2026 compared with 2025.

The report is mildly negative for the growth outlook. The stagnation in quarterly GDP, combined with industrial weakness and a negative contribution from net exports, highlights structural growth challenges. Domestic demand remains the main source of resilience, but the economy is still struggling to generate broader-based growth.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Germany Q3 preliminary GDP +0.2% vs +0.1% q/q expected
item.description:
• Prior +0.3%
  • GDP Y/Y +1.2% vs 1.1% expected
  • Prior +1.0%

Germany's economy expanded by 0.2% q/q in the third quarter of 2026, according to preliminary data from Destatis, extending the recovery seen in the first half of the year. GDP increased by 1.3% y/y in price-adjusted terms, or 1.2% when adjusted for both prices and calendar effects.

However, the underlying details point to a loss of momentum, with the recovery becoming increasingly uneven. Consumer spending made a modest positive contribution, suggesting that domestic demand is holding up, but investment declined, highlighting continued weakness in business activity.

Meanwhile, exports, which provided a significant boost to growth during the first half of the year, lost momentum in Q3. This is particularly relevant for Germany, given its heavy reliance on external demand and the importance of its manufacturing and export sectors.

Overall, the report suggests that Germany's economic recovery is losing some steam. Growth is still positive, although the weaker performance of investment and exports raises questions about how sustainable the recovery will be heading into the final quarter of the year considering all the headwinds from tightening financial conditions and geopolitical shocks.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Spain Q3 GDP growth slows slightly but it's the inflation problem that should worry the ECB
item.description:

  • Prior +0.7%
  • Spain Q3 preliminary GDP +2.7% vs +2.7% y/y expected
  • Prior +2.6%

It is the preliminary report, so there aren't much details to work with here besides the headline figures above.

The quarterly figure does show a bit of a slowdown in Spanish economic growth in the third quarter, albeit marginally. And among the bigger names in the euro area, Spain is still very much punching above its weight in carrying the more optimistic banner for the region.

The only issue is that inflation pressures in Spain is also starting to get out of hand. Headline annual inflation is bordering on 5% in October with core annual inflation holding above 3%. Those numbers are way beyond what the ECB would be comfortable with, running above their 2% price target.

The Spanish GDP report here isn't something to spook markets. But a mild slowdown if coupled with troubling performances in France and perhaps Germany later, that could really ramp up talk of stagflation risks in the euro area especially when paired with the inflation numbers today.

Traders might still lean more favourably on inflation risks prompting the ECB to act in December. But if growth conditions continue to suffer, it might only be a matter of time before the narrative shifts and the focus turns to stagflation risks instead. So, just be wary of that.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Spain inflation remains stubbornly high near 5% as the ECB headache gets worse
item.description:
• Spain October preliminary CPI +4.9% vs +4.9% y/y expected
  • Prior +4.9%
  • Spain October preliminary HICP +4.9% vs +4.9% y/y expected
  • Prior +5.0%

Spanish inflation continues to hover around 5% in October, as the preliminary estimates continue to paint a rather uncomfortable picture for the most part. Headline annual inflation remains steady at 4.9% while the harmonised reading eased marginally to 4.9% as well. So, that's not saying a lot after the run higher in the past few months amid a surge energy prices due to the Middle East conflict.

And with higher oil prices continuing to stick, that will certainly add to the inflation headache in Q4.

Looking at the details, core annual inflation is seen at 3.1% - unchanged compared to September. But at this level, it is still well above what the ECB would be comfortable with as price pressures continue to pull away from the 2% target.

Alongside the earlier report from France, this just continues to reaffirm that the inflation monster is getting bigger and more threatening for the central bank. But at the same time, flagging economic growth conditions will just mean that stagflation risks are also on the rise.

So, that is quite a troubling spot for policymakers to be in as they have to try and deal with price pressures before they get out of hand while avoiding sending the broader economy off a cliff. Tough.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: France inflation heats up again in October, leaving the ECB caught between a rock and a hard place
item.description:
• France October preliminary CPI +3.4% vs +3.2% y/y expected
  • Prior +3.1%
  • France October preliminary HICP +3.8% vs +3.6% y/y expected
  • Prior +3.4%

French inflation is seen accelerating again in October, as the preliminary estimates show headline annual inflation climbing to its highest since December 2023. Yowza.

The main culprit is once again energy prices, as that continues to fuel much of the headline price increase. No pun intended. Of note, energy price inflation was up 24.1% annually in October compared to 21.3% in the month before.

The detailed breakdown shows food price inflation softening slightly to 1.2% in October but services inflation is seen picking up further to 2.7% from 2.4% in the month before. The latter is a real issue as it signals that higher energy prices are starting to spill over more broadly, and that will in turn feed into core inflation as well.

It's not a good look if you're the ECB. France is already struggling economically, not to mention with fiscal headwinds growing stronger by the day. And with inflation pressures starting to heat up as well, that is making for a very stagflationary outlook for Europe's second-largest economy.

For the central bank, this is their biggest issue and risk to tightening policy further. That is especially the case as French bonds are also coming under heavy pressure amid fiscal worries and that could threaten to blow over to the rest of the euro area as well.

It's really a case of damned if you do, damned if you don't for the ECB.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: German import prices surge at fastest pace in nearly four years as energy costs bite
item.description:
• Germany September import prices +2.1% vs +1.8% m/m expected
  • Prior +1.0%
  • Germany September import prices +10.4% vs +10.3% y/y expected
  • Prior +8.3%

Just when Germany thought it had enough economic headaches to deal with, here's another one to add to the pile. This time, the inflation monster is making quite the comeback through the back door.

German import prices for September are seen rosing at their fastest annual pace since November 2022, with the monthly increase also coming in hotter than expected. And surprise, surprise. Not. It is energy that is once again doing much of the damage.

Imported energy prices surged by a whopping 61.8% compared to a year ago, with electricity prices almost doubling (+96.2%) compared to the year before. The US-Iran conflict is definitely leaving its mark on Germany's import bill and businesses aren't exactly getting much breathing room elsewhere either.

Prices for intermediate goods rose 11.1% annually, including a 37.9% increase in copper and 23.4% rise in aluminium. And even if you strip out energy prices, import prices were still up by 5.5% year-on-year in September.

So, what does this tell us?

To start, the details suggest that Germany's imported inflation problem isn't just about expensive oil and gas prices. Higher input costs are spreading across industrial supply chains and that could potentially squeeze manufacturers' margins at a time when the economy can ill afford another setback.

And this also spells trouble for the ECB. Now, import prices aren't the same as consumer prices of course. However, sustained increases in energy and production costs could eventually filter through to households, depending on how much businesses can pass those costs along.

All in all, this will just be another anecdote in reaffirming the prospects of another ECB rate hike in December - especially with markets already pricing in roughly 61% odds of such a move at this juncture.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: BOJ governor Ueda tries to play down inflation victory declaration, says it will be up to the government to call that
item.description:
Further remarks on the day by Ueda:

  • Not yet able to decalre that inflation target has been achieved
  • We think it is mportant for inflation to stably and sustainably hold around 2%
  • BOJ not planning to make a formal declaration at some point that price target has been achieved
  • It is up to government to declare the end of deflation
  • Will not comment on whether the joint accord with the government will be revised or not
  • For now, cannot ignore risk of inflation overshooting
  • Overshooting risks have not necessarily increased compared with a month ago

As a reminder, it was the BOJ outlook report earlier that noted that underlying inflation is generally consistent with the 2% target and is expected to stay there. And Ueda also reaffirmed that view with his earlier comments here. Alongside revising their inflation forecasts higher, it is more or less a victory declaration on inflation. Even Ueda himself said that all members on the board agreed that underlying inflation has reached the 2% target now.

But yet, Ueda wants to play this down instead of use it as a springboard to push more rate hikes. And that says a lot about the current appetite of the BOJ to be more proactive in taking action.

As much as we want to think the BOJ has changed and is becoming more bold, Ueda is serving up a timely reminder here that they would still very much prefer to err on the side of caution and move more slowly instead. Another rate hike in December is very much still up in the air.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: BOJ governor Ueda says will stick to rate hike path in response to latest macro developments
item.description:
In case you missed it, the BOJ left its policy rate unchanged at 1.25% in a 8-1 vote earlier today. And while the decision in itself was widely expected, the central bank finally moved to declare victory on inflation after a hard-fought battle for more than a decade.

Ueda is now following up on that decision and is arguing that the board is sharing a unanimous view on prices at this juncture. His comments:

  • Japan's economy expected to continue growing moderately
  • Underlying inflation at level generally consistent with 2% price stability target, expected to remain at around that level
  • All members agreed that underlying inflation has reached 2% target
  • Cannot condone underlying inflation from becoming higher
  • BOJ will continue to raise policy rate and adjust degree of monetary easing in response to economic activity, prices, and financial developments
  • Will consider adjustment of timing, pace on monetary policy while looking at likelihood of achieving baseline scenarios to the economic, price outlook
  • Need to monitor risks, financial environment and impact on economy, prices a little more (when asked on why the BOJ chose to hold today)
  • However, more important than ever that underlying inflation is not allowed to overshoot 2% target

Well, his comments are certainly leaning more towards the hawkish side but yet the BOJ is not willing to take any action. That pretty much says it all.

The balance of risks has certainly shifted, with policymakers now underscoring the necessity to not let inflation get out of hand. And so the only question now is how willing is the BOJ to step up its game and walk the talk instead of just talking the talk.

Ueda also adds that they will want to be more proactive and will "promptly" adjust policy to steer inflation to 2% rather than "waiting passively". But again, actions speak louder than words.

December remains very much in play but it is clear that the BOJ wants to keep their options open. The only issue though in waiting too long is that they might miss their timing, even more so when Japan prime minister Takaichi is going to have another opportunity to reshape the board next year. And that could very well make it even tougher for the BOJ to pursue any further tightening measures.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.
